name: Iris Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a dragline at a big open-cut coal mine. A dragline is a crane the size of an apartment block with a bucket on a cable, and it strips off the dirt and rock above the coal seam. I swing the bucket out, drag it back full, swing it over and dump it on the spoil pile, about a thousand times a shift. You have to feel the bucket through the controls, and a bad swing can put two hundred tonnes of steel where it shouldn't be.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thirty-five years at the mine, nineteen on the dragline. I'm the senior operator and I train anyone new who comes up. My husband Tomas was a fitter at the same mine until he retired, and our son Joel's a fitter there now. We go to the same church we were married in, and most of the congregation works at the mine or is married to someone who does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I knew it. Every few years the head office sends someone with a new gadget, and it ends up gathering dust. I'd say it after church and at the crib table. I'm not on the internet, Joel's wife does that for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd thank God for it. I've got three or four years left and I want to finish them in my own seat. Tomas and I have the house, the savings and his pension, so we'd be very comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just keep working. Keep training the young ones the way I was trained, by an old man named Frank who never let me touch the controls for the first month. I wouldn't touch any AI, I've never used it and I don't see the need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Peaceful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Frank teach you that you still pass on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Patience. He'd say the machine is bigger than you, so let it do the work and don't fight it. I still say that to every trainee, word for word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the mine that worries you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coal itself. The politicians in the city want us closed anyway, AI or no AI. That's a bigger worry for this town than any robot.

S0.say: I'd say I knew it, because every few years head office sends a new gadget that ends up gathering dust. I'd say it after church and at the crib table, since I'm not on the internet.
S0.think: Privately I'd thank God for it, with three or four years left to finish in my own seat. With the house, savings and Tomas's pension, we'd be very comfortable.
S0.do: Keeps working and training young operators the way Frank trained her. Stays away from AI tools, which she has never used.
S0.quote: Let it do the work and don't fight it.
S0.fieldNote: Iris's world is tightly bound together: work, family, church and town all centre on the mine. Her real long-term worry is political pressure to close coal, not AI. She passes on her mentor's words exactly, which says a lot about how she values tradition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company's chasing shortcuts again. People who've never stood on a spoil pile deciding what we can do without. I'd say it at work and to anyone at church who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think they'd go after the trucks and the drills first, and maybe leave the dragline for a while. It's too big and too dear to let a computer crash it. But Joel's job worries me, because the machines he fixes might start reporting their own faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep working. I wouldn't sign up for any computer training unless I had to, and if I had to, I'd think hard about whether to just retire. I'd wait and see what the company actually does, not what it announces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much as for Joel and the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Joel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to make himself the fitter they can't do without. Learn every machine on site, the old ones and the new ones. That's what his father did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd advise Joel to learn the new machines but you wouldn't. Is that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it is. But he's thirty-two and I'm fifty-eight. There's a time to learn and a time to hand over, and I'm in the handing over part.

S1.say: I'd say the company is chasing shortcuts again, with people who've never stood on a spoil pile deciding what we can do without. I'd say it at work and at church.
S1.think: Privately I think the trucks and drills go first and the dragline is too big and costly to risk on a computer. But Joel's job worries me if machines start reporting their own faults.
S1.do: Keeps her head down and keeps working, avoiding computer training unless forced, in which case she would consider retiring. Waits to see what the company actually does.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly for Joel and the town.
S1.quote: There's a time to learn and a time to hand over, and I'm in the handing over part.
S1.fieldNote: Iris accepted the contradiction between her advice to Joel and her own refusal gracefully. Her worry is family first, then town. She is sceptical of company announcements and would judge by actions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when billionaires and city people run everything. Nobody asked the families in towns like ours. I'd say it after church, and I'd sign any petition going round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me. Not my money, we'd be fine. But Joel has three little ones and a mortgage, and half the people in our church would be out of work within two years. I don't know what this town is without the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire as soon as they started bringing the machines in, I wouldn't stay to watch it. Then I'd help Joel and his family, with money if they need it, and I'd tell him they could move in with us for a while if it came to that. And I'd help the church set up something for families, meals and the like, because that's what you do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. I'd pray a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the two-year timeline change things for you, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is too fast for a family to turn around. Joel can't retrain, sell his house and move in two years without losing everything. With ten years, he could see it coming and get his family somewhere safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned not wanting government handouts in the past. Would you take help in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Joel to have work, not a cheque. But if it's this fast, I'd swallow my pride for my grandchildren. I just wouldn't like it.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when billionaires and city people run everything without asking families in towns like ours. I'd say it after church and sign any petition going round.
S2.think: Privately it frightens me, not for our money but for Joel with three little ones and a mortgage, and half our church out of work. I don't know what this town is without the mine.
S2.do: Retires as soon as the machines arrive, then supports Joel's family with money and offers them a place to live. Helps the church organise meals and support for families, and signs petitions.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake and praying a lot.
S2.quote: I don't know what this town is without the mine.
S2.fieldNote: Iris's own finances are safe, but this picture threatens everything she values: family, church and town. Her fear is real and comes through her son and grandchildren. She would accept government help for her grandchildren while making clear she'd prefer work to a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, that nobody asked us. But I'd also say, families, start planning now. I'd say that from the church hall if they let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd see the start of it before I retire, at sixty-three. It's still fast for Joel, but he'd have time to think. I'd still worry, but I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working until I was ready, maybe sixty-one, and then retire. I'd sit down with Joel and his wife and talk about whether they should pay down the mortgage faster or look for work somewhere else. I'd put some money aside for the grandkids' schooling, so whatever happens they've got that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the two-year one, but still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years give your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to pay down Joel's house. Time for him to decide whether to stay or go. With two years he'd be caught out, with five he can choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want Joel to move away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd hate it. Our family's been in this town four generations. But I'd rather visit my grandchildren somewhere else than watch them grow up in a dying town.

S3.say: I'd say again that nobody asked us, but also tell families to start planning now. I'd say it from the church hall if they let me.
S3.think: Privately five years means I'd see the start of it before retiring at sixty-three. It's still fast for Joel, but he'd have time to think, and I'd still sleep.
S3.do: Keeps working until about 61, then retires. Talks with Joel and his wife about paying down their mortgage or finding work elsewhere, and sets money aside for the grandchildren's schooling.
S3.feel: Anxious, less than in the two-year picture but still present.
S3.quote: I'd rather visit my grandchildren somewhere else than watch them grow up in a dying town.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time softens Iris from alarmed to anxious, mainly because it gives Joel choices. Her willingness to see her son move away despite four generations in the town shows how seriously she takes this. She thinks in terms of family plans rather than politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for families to prepare, if they're sensible. I'd still say the city people are deciding for us. But at least there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be long retired. For Joel, it's ten years to plan, and that's a lot. I'd mostly worry about the town and the church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retire around sixty-one or sixty-two, as I'd planned. I'd encourage Joel to start learning the new machines early, the way his father would have. And I'd keep helping out at church, because whatever happens to the mine, people will need each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly at peace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the church do, in a town where the mine runs itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe it'd matter more, not less. When people lose their work, they need somewhere to belong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most, if you saw the dragline running without anyone in it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bucket swinging out over the pit at sunrise, and the whole cab shaking when it bites in. I'd drive past and look at it. I'd probably have to pull over.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for sensible families to prepare, though city people are still deciding for us. At least there's time.
S4.think: Privately I'd be long retired, and ten years gives Joel plenty of time to plan. I'd mostly worry about the town and the church.
S4.do: Retires around 61 or 62 as planned and encourages Joel to learn the new machines early. Keeps helping at church so people have support.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, mostly at peace.
S4.quote: When people lose their work, they need somewhere to belong.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Iris relaxes about her family and focuses on the church as a place of belonging. Her vivid image of the dragline at sunrise showed how much the work means to her identity. She keeps blaming distant decision-makers but with less heat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028. Because of Joel and his babies, and because the town wouldn't have time to find its feet. What would help is real work for people like Joel, apprenticeships and jobs, not just a cheque in the mail.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about church. Everyone talks about jobs and money. Nobody talks about what holds a town together when the work goes, and for us it's the church and the football club.

headlineQuote: Nobody talks about what holds a town together when the work goes, and for us it's the church and the football club.
portrait: Iris Santos is a 58-year-old senior dragline operator at an open-cut coal mine, with thirty-five years on site, a husband retired from the same mine and a son, Joel, working there as a fitter. She is devout, rooted in a four-generation mining town, avoids new technology entirely and has never used AI. Her money is safe, so her fears run through her family, church and town. She is calm in AI Plateau, uneasy in Steady Disruption and alarmed in AGI by 2028, when Joel and half her congregation could lose work. She blames billionaires and city decision-makers and wants real work and apprenticeships rather than handouts.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her son Joel and his young family, and the town, would have no time to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: Real work and apprenticeships for people like her son, rather than just a cheque in the mail.
